Choosing a tech stack you won't regret in three years

EngineeringBy the OneClicq team9 November 20266 min read

The technology behind a business application is a long-term commitment. A good choice fades into the background; a poor one shows up years later as slow delivery, hiring trouble and expensive rewrites.

Ask these questions before comparing tools

  1. What does the product need to do? A content website, a transaction-heavy ERP, a real-time dashboard and a mobile app have different needs.
  2. Who will maintain it? If you have an in-house team, their existing skills matter more than any benchmark.
  3. How big will it get? Plan for realistic growth over three years, not for a scale you may never reach.
  4. What must it connect to? Payment gateways, accounting software, government portals and existing databases all have preferred integration methods.
  5. What are the rules? Data residency, security standards and audit requirements can rule options in or out.

Prefer boring, well-supported technology

Mature tools with long support lifecycles, large communities and plenty of available developers are usually the safest choice for business software. For example:

  • Frontend: React or Angular for web applications; Flutter or native Android and iOS for mobile.
  • Backend: .NET, Node.js or Python, each with strong frameworks and long-term support releases.
  • Database: PostgreSQL or SQL Server for most business data; add specialised stores only when there is a clear need.
  • Cloud: AWS or Azure, using managed services to reduce the work of running servers.

New tools can be excellent, but every unusual choice adds a hiring and maintenance cost. Use them where they give a clear advantage, not by default.

Check the total cost, not just the licence

Include hosting, monitoring, third-party services, developer salaries and the cost of upgrades over three years. A free framework that needs scarce specialists can cost more than a licensed product your team already knows.

Avoid lock-in where it matters

Some lock-in is fine if it saves real effort. Keep the most valuable parts portable: your data in standard formats, your business logic in your own code, and integrations behind clear APIs. That way you can change a vendor without rebuilding the business.

Prove it with a small spike

Before committing, build a thin slice of the riskiest feature with the proposed stack, for example the integration with your payment gateway or a report over real data volumes. A week of real code answers questions that months of debate cannot.

A simple scoring sheet

Score each option from 1 to 5 on: fit for the product, team skills, hiring market, maturity and support, integration needs, security and compliance, and three-year cost. Weight the criteria that matter most to your business. The highest score is rarely the newest option, and that is usually a good sign.
